finding.claim: Mass assignment: PUT /me copies the entire request body onto req.user via Object.assign and persists it, letting an authenticated user overwrite any field (e.g. role, isAdmin, email, passwordHash) on their own record.

trace.note: All body keys copied onto req.user with no allowlist

finding.guards_checked: No schema validation, no field allowlist, no protected-property check in users.js. Auth middleware that sets req.user is outside the directory and unverified.

verdict.guard_found: none in users.js: no schema validation, field allowlist, or protected-property check between req.body (users.js:4) and Object.assign (users.js:5). The auth middleware that sets req.user and the req.store implementation are not in the directory, so any filtering there cannot be checked.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: users.js:4 takes req.body, users.js:5 assigns all of it onto req.user, users.js:6 saves it, and users.js:7 returns it. Whether this is exploitable depends on fields outside the directory: whether the user record has privileged fields like role or isAdmin (not visible here), and whether req.store.save or a schema layer filters writes (not visible here), so the impact cannot be confirmed from the available code.

finding.claim: Prototype-chain variant of F1: a body with a __proto__ key triggers the __proto__ setter during Object.assign, changing req.user's prototype so inherited reads (e.g. req.user.isAdmin) can return attacker-chosen values. Not verified by execution.
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, req.body) (users.js:5); later inherited property reads on req.user

trace.note: JSON.parse yields an own key named __proto__
Object.assign uses [[Set]], invoking the __proto__ setter and replacing the prototype
save may serialize only own properties, so persistence is uncertain

finding.guards_checked: None in users.js. Node test was declined, so this is based on the language spec only.

verdict.guard_found: none in users.js. The only in-file controls are none; req.user and req.body come from middleware not present in this file, and no inherited-property authorization check appears after the assign.
verdict.reason: The trace is wrong at users.js:4, which is the `router.put("/me", ...)` declaration and contains no JSON.parse (body parsing happens outside this file); and at users.js:5-7 nothing reads an inherited property like isAdmin after Object.assign, while res.json and req.store.save only serialize own properties, so the prototype change has no demonstrated effect here.

finding.claim: Profile update overwrites stored displayName/bio with undefined when a field is omitted, and accepts unvalidated types and unbounded lengths.
finding.source: displayName and bio from req.body of PUT /me/profile (users.js:11)
finding.sink: Object.assign(req.user, { displayName, bio }) (users.js:12) followed by req.store.save (users.js:13)

trace.note: Destructure yields undefined for omitted fields
Omitted fields overwrite existing values with undefined; non-string values pass through

finding.guards_checked: No type checks, length limits, or validation in users.js. Store behaviour with object-valued fields is unknown.

verdict.guard_found: none in users.js. Line 11 destructures req.body, line 12 Object.assign copies undefined values onto req.user, line 13 saves it. No validation or length checks exist. The auth middleware that sets req.user is not in the directory, so I could not confirm it.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: Object.assign at users.js:12 does overwrite stored fields with undefined when omitted, and the value is saved at users.js:13. But the write targets req.user (users.js:12-13), which is the caller's own record, so an authenticated user can only corrupt or bloat their own profile. That is a correctness and input-validation issue, not a security vulnerability, because the attacker already holds that power. The verdict would change only if req.user could refer to another user's record, which the code here does not show.
